newsitem.title: USA: Industries should disclose toxic chemical uses - EPA.
newsitem.headline: Industries should disclose toxic chemical uses - EPA.

text.p: The Environmental Protection Agency Wednesday proposed forcing a number of industries to disclose how they use toxic chemicals, expanding a community-right-to-know programme on industrial toxins.
The plan would apply to industries currently forced to report on the toxic chemicals they release into the environment in a programme called the Toxic Release Inventory.

"The expansion we are considering would give the public the right to know not just which chemicals come out of local industrial facilities, but which chemicals go into their neighbourhoods and how they are used," EPA Administrator Carol Browner said in a statement.
"Putting information about local pollution into the hands of the public is the single most effective, common-sense tool available for protecting public health and the environment," Browner said.

Currently 20 categories of industries covering some 23,000 facilities must make Toxic Release Inventory reports on their chemical emissions, and the Clinton administration has proposed expanding the categories and adding another 6,400 facilities.

Reporting on how industries use toxic chemicals "would expand public information available on toxic chemicals that enter local industrial facilities; the amounts of chemicals transformed into products and waste; and toxic chemicals that leave the facility," the EPA statement said.

President Clinton last month said the administration intended to expand chemical emissions reporting, a programme disliked by many of the regulated industries and which a number of Republicans in Congress sought to curb.
A spokeswoman for the National Association of Manufacturers said the industry group was studying the plan.
"In general NAM opposes expansion of the TRI to include chemcial uses," she said.
